newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany to allow share buybacks, 10 pct limit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany to allow share buybacks, 10 pct limit.

text.p: An imminent liberalisation of German share laws will simplify share buybacks, allowing companies to repurchase up to 10 percent of their own capital, a senior Justice Ministry official said on Monday.

The move is part of a package of reforms designed to further increase shareholder value, a major buzzword in Germany, which is trying hard to promote an equity culture and attract more foreign interest to its financial markets.

Justice Ministry state secretary Rainer Funke, who heads a government working group developing the laws, which are expected to be implemented in 1998, told a news conference that share buybacks would give German capital markets a much needed boost.

"The many investigations of share buybacks in the U.S. have yielded positive results for all those involved ... The company achieves the advantages it needs. The shareholders, both those who sell and those who hold, benefit from higher prices."
Legal restrictions currently make share buybacks a near impossibility in Germany, except under emergency conditions.

Despite intensive lobbying from top corporate officials, concern has persisted that company heads could try to use the buyback option to outmanoeuvre opposing shareholders or give privileges to others.
Funke said Germany's liberalised laws would carry certain restrictions and that there was no intention to completely follow the more liberalised U.S. example.
The German buyback proposal was deliberately framed on the lines of a European Union directive of 1976, which restricts buyback rights to 10 percent of capital.
Funke also said the new share laws would maintain the status quo on several other peculiarities of German corporate practice which are viewed with some suspicion internationally.

For example, he said the government did not plan to introduce legal restrictions on corporate shareholdings by banks, a thorny issue which has attracted much international criticism of the level of influence banks have on firms.

Funke said the government had failed to reach a consensus on this issue, partly because of possible constitutional infringements and partly because such restrictions would not succeed in eliminating possible conflicts of interest.

A more effective measure would be to improve the transparency of bank shareholdings, he said. A recent law, for example, has required banks to release details of their corporate holdings once they exceed five percent.
Germany will also leave unaltered the right of company management board members to hold positions on up to 10 supervisory boards of other firms, Funke said.

This right "does not just entail risks for the companies but also significant advantages, especially synergy effects," he argued, pointing out that the system allowed many companies to benefit from one individual's expertise.
The share law proposals are still at an initial stage and will be reviewed on a regular basis over the coming months.
However, the progress so far is likely to please German industrialists, who have argued for years that buybacks are an effective means of rewarding shareholders and tackling excess liquidity.
